To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the growth factor-induced activation of hepatocyte morphogenesis on organotypic matrices is substrate-specific, with a cooperative effect on aggregation kinetics, and that the growth factor stimulation of hepatocyte function is substrate-sensitive.
growth factor stimulation of hepatocytes cultured in 3D on Matrigel substrates selectively induces or represses liver-specific function depending on the mechanical compliance of Matrigel.
the kinetics of hepatocyte aggregation and liver-specific function are differentially controlled by growth factor stimulation and mechanical compliance of the culture substrate.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design and analysis of biomimetic culture substrates for the study of hepatocyte morphogenesis and liver-specific function.
elucidating the mechanisms that regulate the morphogenetic and functional plasticity of hepatocyte populations cultured on organotypically defined substrates.
the design of tissue engineering microenvironments for controlled induction and repression of liver-specific function in hepatocyte cultures.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
growth factor stimulation can selectively enhance or repress hepatocyte function depending on the mechanical properties of the culture substrate.

the mechanical properties of the culture substrate can be used to control the extent of growth factor stimulation of hepatocyte function, thereby enabling the development of novel strategies for the design of 3D tissue culture systems.
the mechanical compliance of culture matrices is an important parameter to consider for controlling the functional outcome of hepatocytes in culture.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

growth factor stimulation, when combined with the appropriate mechanical compliance of the culture substrate, is a powerful tool for controlling the kinetics and extent of aggregation, which in turn can be utilized to selectively induce or repressed liver-specific functions in hepatocytes.
the mechanical compliance of a matrix can be used to selectively control the kinetics of aggregation and the extent of functional repression of hepatocytes in response to growth factor stimulation.

hepatocyte function is regulated by the mechanical properties of the culture substrate and growth factor activation of aggregation, in a manner dependent on the mechanical compliance of that substrate.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the mechanical properties of the extracellular matrix and the mechanical cues that it provides to the cell play a critical role in regulating the response of cells to growth factor stimulation, which is important in the design of biomaterials for tissue engineering applications.

the mechanical properties of the substrate and the nature of growth factor stimulation are two independent parameters that can be used to control cellular aggregation and liver-specific function in a synergistic manner.
the mechanosensory nature of the cellular environment is an important parameter in the design of tissue culture substrates to achieve optimal cellular function in tissue reconstruction therapies.
